A 4-year-old girl of Turkish ancestry was brought to the emergency department for progressive unsteadiness and recurrent falls over the preceding 5 days. Five days earlier she had first noted staggering and grabbing for support to avoid falls; during her initial fall she sustained a nasal bridge laceration that required suturing. There was no prior medical history. On examination she was alert (GCS 15), afebrile, and appeared well; the nasal bridge wound was clean. Both external ear canals were obstructed by effusion and cerumen; the remainder of the neurologic and physical examination, including cranial-nerve testing, was age-appropriate. Routine blood tests were unremarkable.  
 Three-month history of “ear problems” was elicited: initial diagnosis of otitis media with effusion and tympanic perforation treated with antibiotics led to partial resolution. On current otoscopic examination, the left tympanic membrane was intact without effusion; the right external canal was occluded by polypoid tissue and purulent secretion. A Frenzel’s examination showed no nystagmus.  
 Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and temporal bones revealed bilateral osteolysis of the mastoids, superior and lateral semicircular canals, and the right external auditory canal, plus a separate osteolytic lesion in the dorsal left parietal bone. There was also adenoid hypertrophy and mild sinus mucosal thickening.  
 Brainstem evoked response audiometry demonstrated a threshold of 40 dB with normal wave latencies on the left and an 80 dB threshold with prolonged wave I latency on the right, indicating profound right-sided hearing loss.
